ai.literal: One may beg, those worthy of being begged from if one sees; if they withhold, their blame, one's own blame it is not.
ai.translation: One may beg if they meet those who are worthy of giving; if those givers withhold their wealth, the blame is theirs, not the beggar's.
ai.modern: இரந்து கேட்பதற்குத் தகுதியானவர்களைக் கண்டால் அவரிடம் இரந்து கேட்கலாம்; அவ்வாறு கேட்டபோது அவர் கொடுக்காமல் மறைத்தால், அது அவருக்குப் பழியே தவிர, கேட்பவருக்குப் பழி அன்று.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the ethics of asking for help and where the shame of refusal lies. The poet suggests that begging is acceptable if one approaches those who are genuinely worthy and capable of giving. If these wealthy individuals choose to hide their resources and refuse to help, the moral disgrace belongs entirely to them. The person in need who asked for help bears no blame or shame in this situation.

ai.literal: Pleasure to a person begging, those things begged, pain without causing, if they come.
ai.translation: Even begging becomes a pleasure to a person if the things they ask for are given without causing any pain or distress.
ai.modern: ஒருவருக்குப் பிறரிடம் இரந்து கேட்பது இன்பமாகும், அவ்வாறு இரந்து கேட்ட பொருள்கள் துன்பம் தராமல் கிடைக்குமானால்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that the act of begging, which is usually painful and humiliating, can actually bring joy under a specific condition. That condition is when the requested items (இரந்தவை) are given freely and gracefully, without causing any distress (துன்பம் உறாஅ) or humiliation to the seeker. The key phrase 'துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்' highlights that the manner of giving determines the emotional outcome of the request. When met with immediate and painless generosity, the act of asking becomes a source of happiness rather than shame.

ai.literal: Standing before those who know their duty and have a heart without concealment, even begging possesses a unique beauty.
ai.translation: Standing and asking for help before those who know their duty and possess a heart free from withholding has a unique beauty of its own.
ai.modern: ஒளித்துவைக்கும் குணம் இல்லாத நெஞ்சத்தையும், தம் கடமையை அறியும் தன்மையையும் உடையவர் முன்னே நின்று இரந்து கேட்பதும் ஒரு தனி அழகைப் பெற்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that asking for help is not always a matter of shame; it can have its own grace under the right circumstances. When a person stands and asks (இரப்பும்) before those who do not hide what they have (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின்) and who understand their social duty to give (கடனறிவார்), the act of asking becomes dignified. The beauty (ஏஎர்) of this interaction lies in the mutual understanding between a needy person and a generous, dutiful giver. Thus, the poet elevates the act of seeking help when it is directed at the truly noble.

ai.literal: Even begging resembles indeed giving, towards those who do not know hiding even in a dream.
ai.translation: Begging from those who do not know how to hide their wealth, even in their dreams, is as pleasant as giving itself.
ai.modern: கனவிலும் பிறருக்குக் கொடுப்பதை மறைக்கத் தெரியாதவர்களிடம் சென்று இரப்பதும், பிறருக்குக் கொடுப்பதைப் போன்ற பெருமை உடையதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that begging is not always a degrading act; its nature depends entirely on whom one asks. When a person begs from generous souls who cannot even conceive of hiding their wealth or refusing a request, even in their dreams, that act of receiving becomes as beautiful and dignified as giving itself. The key word 'கரத்தல்' refers to the act of concealing one's resources to avoid giving, and 'தேற்றாதார்' describes those who are completely incapable of such deceit. Thus, asking from such noble givers brings no shame, only joy.

ai.literal: Because of the existence in the world of those who do not hide, those who beg undertake to stand in front.
ai.translation: It is only because there are people in this world who do not hide their wealth that others undertake the act of standing before them to beg.
ai.modern: பிறருக்குக் கொடுக்காமல் மறைக்காதவர்கள் இவ்வுலகில் இருப்பதால்தான், இரப்பவர்கள் அவர்களிடம் நேரில் நின்று யாசிப்பதை மேற்கொள்கிறார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the social dynamic that keeps the act of asking for charity alive. The poet states that begging is only practiced because there exist generous people ('கரப்பிலார்') in the world ('வையகத்து') who do not hide their resources when asked. It is this existence ('உண்மையால்') that gives the needy the hope and courage to stand face-to-face ('கண்ணின்று') and make their request. Without the presence of such open-handed givers, the act of begging ('இரப்பவர் மேற்கொள்வது') would disappear entirely.

ai.literal: If one sees those who do not have the evil of concealing wealth, all the affliction of poverty will perish at once.
ai.translation: If those who ask meet people who are free from the mean habit of hiding their wealth, all the misery of their poverty will vanish at once.
ai.modern: தம்மிடம் உள்ளதை மறைத்து வைக்கும் தீய குணம் இல்லாதவர்களைக் கண்டால், வறுமையினால் உண்டாகும் துன்பங்கள் அனைத்தும் உடனே நீங்கிவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the profound relief a needy person feels upon encountering a truly generous giver. The word 'karappu' refers to the act of hiding or withholding one's wealth when someone asks for help, which is described here as an 'iṭumpai' (an evil or painful trait). When a seeker finds someone free from this withholding nature ('karappiṭumpai illārai'), their own 'nirappiṭumpai' (the misery of poverty) instantly disappears. The mere sight of such a noble person brings immediate comfort, as the seeker knows their distress is already resolved.

ai.literal: Without despising and mocking, those who give if one sees, rejoicing, the mind deep within delighting possesses.
ai.translation: If one meets givers who give without despising or mocking, the mind rejoices and feels a deep, inward delight.
ai.modern: இகழ்ந்து ஒதுக்காமலும் எள்ளி நகையாடாமலும் கொடை கொடுப்பவரைக் கண்டால், இரப்பவரின் உள்ளம் மகிழ்ந்து தன் ஆழத்திற்குள் இன்பமடையும் தன்மை உடையதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the emotional experience of a person in need when they encounter a truly respectful giver. The words 'இகழ்ந்து' (despising) and 'எள்ளாது' (without mocking) describe the ideal attitude of a benefactor who does not look down upon the beggar. When such dignified givers are found ('காணின்'), the seeker's mind ('உள்ளம்') does not just feel superficial relief; it rejoices ('மகிழ்ந்து') and experiences a profound, secret joy deep within ('உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து'). The poet emphasizes that the manner of giving is far more valuable than the material gift itself.

ai.literal: If those who beg are not there, the cool, wide, great world is like a wooden puppet going and coming.
ai.translation: If there were no beggars to ask for alms, the movements of people in this vast, cool world would be like the mere coming and going of wooden puppets.
ai.modern: இரந்து கேட்பவர்கள் இல்லையென்றால், குளிர்ந்த இடத்தையுடைய இந்த பெரிய உலகத்தில் வாழும் மக்களின் இயக்கம், மரப்பாவை தானாகவே சென்று வருவது போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the social and human value of giving and receiving. The author suggests that if there were no people who ask for help, the act of giving charity would cease to exist. Without the interplay of giving and receiving, human life would lose its warmth, empathy, and social connection. Consequently, the people moving about in this vast, cool world would be no different from lifeless wooden puppets controlled by strings, moving mechanically without true human spirit.

ai.literal: Among those who give, what will be the glory, if those who desire receiving by asking do not exist?
ai.translation: What glory can there be for those who give, if there are no people who desire to receive by asking?
ai.modern: இரந்து கேட்பதை விரும்புகின்றவர்கள் இல்லாதபோது, கொடுப்பவர்களிடம் என்ன பெருமை உண்டாகும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the codependent relationship between the giver and the receiver. The author asks what renown or glory can exist for generous givers if there are no people who wish to ask for and receive alms. The word 'தோற்றம்' refers to the visible glory or renown of being a benefactor, while 'மேவார்' refers to those who desire or undertake the act of asking. Without the receiver, the virtue of giving cannot manifest, showing that the asker plays an essential role in the cycle of charity.

ai.literal: He who begs, not getting angry is required; the distress of poverty, even itself indeed, is sufficient witness.
ai.translation: One who begs must not get angry when refused; the distress of his own poverty is itself a sufficient witness to his helpless state.
ai.modern: இரப்பவர் பிறர் தமக்குக் கொடாவிட்டாலும் கோபிக்காமல் இருக்க வேண்டும்; அவருடைய வறுமைத் துன்பமே அதற்குப் போதுமான சான்றாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet advises those who are forced to beg to maintain patience and avoid anger when they are turned away. The poet explains that the beggar's own state of poverty and the suffering it brings ('nirappu iṭumpai') serve as a sufficient witness ('kari') to their helplessness. Getting angry at others who do not give is pointless, as the beggar's own destitute condition already proves their lack of power or standing to demand anything. Thus, accepting one's situation without resentment is the only dignified path left.
